summary.name: Consequences of SLO violations (CRE life lessons)
summary.one_liner: A Google Cloud blog post by Alex Bramley explaining why teams should write a policy for how SREs and developers respond to SLO (service level objective) violations, and what that policy's components should be.
keywords: how to respond when slo is missed
use_cases: Writing an SLO violation response policy
Deciding when to page oncall for error budget burn
Setting escalation levels between SRE and dev teams
Balancing feature releases against reliability work
Learning SRE practices for service reliability
summary.what_it_does: The post argues that an SRE team and its partner development teams should document a policy describing how they respond to SLO violations. It recommends grouping violations into a few severity buckets based on how much error budget has been burned over what time horizon, and tying bucket boundaries to SLO-based alerts such as paging when a set share of weekly error budget burns in an hour. It lists consequence categories: notifying oncall and the dev team, escalating to dev teams with expected action, restricting risky releases and experiments until back within SLO, and in extreme cases handing back operational responsibility for a service. It is conceptual guidance, not a tool, and says a follow-up post will show a real Google SRE team's policy.
notable: Recommends grouping SLO violations into severity buckets based on cumulative error budget burn over time
Describes escalation versus notification and when to block releases
Discusses revoking SRE support for a service as a last resort
Written by a Google Cloud Customer Reliability Engineer, archived from the Google Cloud Platform Blog (January 2018)
caveats: Describes general guidance; the specific Google SRE team policy is deferred to a later post and is not included here
Archived page from January 2018; the page text does not say whether the advice is current
